text: # ReproParcel — Product Requirements Document

heading: 2. Problem and community value
text: ## 2. Problem and community value

heading: 2. Problem and community value
text: ### 2.1 Problem statement

heading: 2. Problem and community value
text: “Something is broken” reports usually lack the app build, affected screen, preceding actions and sanitized diagnostic context. Developers spend time asking follow-up questions; agents receive prose without enough grounding to identify the relevant source code. Screenshots may accidentally expose personal data, while always-on recording increases privacy and performance costs.

heading: 2. Problem and community value
text: The useful contribution is **not another dashboard or a claim to be the first bug reporter**. It is a small, inspectable native Android SDK plus an open evidence format and local tools that work independently of a particular SaaS, model or IDE.

heading: 2. Problem and community value

heading: 2. Problem and community value

The product must validate that portability and lightweight local operation are valuable enough to justify another library.

heading: 2. Problem and community value
text: ### 2.3 Why awbuilds can execute this

heading: 2. Problem and community value
text: A private Kotlin/Compose host application provides existing privacy-sensitive workflows and real release-build constraints. It is an appropriate integration proving ground, **not a source of real financial test fixtures**. The initial audience is AGPL-compatible apps and teams willing to satisfy copyleft requirements; proprietary SDK adoption is not assumed.

heading: 3. Vision, goals and success criteria
text: ### 3.1 Full vision

heading: 3. Vision, goals and success criteria
text: A user reports a bug in context. ReproParcel captures only configured and permitted evidence, explains omissions, lets the user review exactly what will leave the device, and produces a self-contained parcel. A developer can inspect it offline. A coding agent can read structured evidence through a read-only adapter, verify build provenance and propose a change under the host project's normal approval rules.

heading: 3. Vision, goals and success criteria

heading: 3. Vision, goals and success criteria
text: **Actionable-report rate:** reports that allow a maintainer to begin a grounded investigation without asking for basic build/screen information, divided by reports reviewed in an opted-in pilot. heading: 3. Vision, goals and success criteria
text: ### 3.4 Non-goals

heading: 3. Vision, goals and success criteria

heading: 4. Users and use cases
text: ### 4.2 Primary use cases

heading: 4. Users and use cases
text: **UC-01 — Visual defect.** A tester sees an overlapping button. They open Report a problem, capture an approved region, mark the overlap, state the expected behavior, review the parcel and export it. The developer receives bounds, device configuration and build metadata, not merely a screenshot.

heading: 4. Users and use cases
text: **UC-02 — Action has no effect.** A tester taps Save and nothing happens. Explicit host-integrated breadcrumbs show the safe action ID and screen transition history. Network metadata may show a failed request if the host enabled the optional adapter. Entered form values are not recorded by default.

heading: 4. Users and use cases
text: **UC-03 — Offline report.** A user creates a report without connectivity. An opted-in draft is retained locally in encrypted form. The user can later export it; no automatic upload occurs in v1. If secure storage is unavailable, the SDK offers an in-memory report rather than falling back to plaintext.

heading: 4. Users and use cases
notes: Sensitive-finance policy and text-only fallback implemented
text: **UC-04 — Sensitive finance screen.** A private host application's development build uses synthetic transactions. In a production integration, finance-specific privacy policies exclude amounts, account data and original messages. If safe image masking cannot be established, the report remains useful with a description and approved metadata while omitting the image and semantic text.

heading: 4. Users and use cases
text: **UC-05 — Agent-assisted triage.** A maintainer imports an approved parcel into a chosen local directory. A read-only MCP server returns the manifest, redacted events and approved image. The agent checks the commit, explains uncertainty and proposes a fix; tests and normal source-control review determine whether the fix is accepted.

heading: 4. Users and use cases
text: **UC-06 — Evidence unavailable.** A protected window, unsupported Compose version or capture timeout prevents collection. The SDK returns a typed omission reason and keeps the report form usable. It does not bypass protection or claim a complete tree.

heading: 4. Users and use cases
text: **UC-07 — SDK malfunction.** An injected collector, lifecycle callback or disk operation fails. The affected feature degrades safely; the host remains operational; SDK diagnostics record only sanitized error codes.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: ## 6. User and developer journeys

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: ### 6.1 Reporter flow

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 1. Host app enables reporting according to its settings and privacy notice. Nothing starts just because a library class is loaded.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 2. User activates an accessible manual entry point or a configured foreground-only shake gesture.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 3. A single report session begins. Eligible on-screen evidence is snapshotted before the reporter obscures it; collector failures become omissions.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 4. Reporter shows description, expected behavior and actual behavior. User marks an allowed image with arrows, pen or opaque privacy masks.

evidence: Text/image review and privacy note; full category/retention panel incomplete
heading: 6. User and developer journeys
notes: Review shows text/image, evidence counts, export method and retention; image category removable
text: 5. User sees evidence categories, redacted image and text, capture limitations, the chosen export method and retention information. They can remove optional categories. For system sharing, explain that the receiving app/recipient is selected next; do not claim recipient-specific approval before the chooser opens.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 6. Finalization revalidates policy and creates the exact export artifact. If its contents change after review, approval is invalidated and review repeats. Artifact approval and destination selection are separate steps.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 7. User opens Android's system share UI, or selects a save destination with the Storage Access Framework. A cancelled SAF operation leaves the host unaffected. Generic sharing cannot reliably report receiving-app completion/cancellation or confirm receipt.

evidence: FileSaved vs ShareLaunched; UI text; tests
heading: 6. User and developer journeys
notes: Reporter has an explicit local-drafts/cache delete control and outcome
text: 8. UI distinguishes “Share chooser opened” from a confirmed local “File saved.” It never reports “Maintainer received it” without a verified delivery contract. Local encrypted drafts can be deleted from the reporter.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: No consent checkbox is preselected for external transfer. Reporting must remain accessible without shaking a device or annotating an image.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: ### 6.2 Developer integration

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 1. Review the AGPL obligations and compatibility notice before adopting the library.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 2. Add only the artifacts needed. Initialize explicitly from the host's application lifecycle and register the current activity safely.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 3. Provide build metadata and safe screen/action IDs. Configure evidence categories; screenshot/semantic text collection is off until a host capture/privacy policy is supplied.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 4. Add a manual reporter entry point. Optionally register foreground shake detection, a structured log sink and the OkHttp metadata adapter.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 5. Mark sensitive regions and excluded screens. Keep the policy close to the feature that owns the data.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 6. Run the integration's privacy fixtures, minified-release smoke, lifecycle tests and resource budget checks.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 7. Update the host privacy policy and, where applicable, store disclosures before enabling production collection/export. The host's existing privacy promises must not be weakened silently.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: The baseline SDK must not force Hilt, Room, a navigation library, Google Play Services or a particular network stack into the host app.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: ### 6.3 Agent workflow

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 1. Maintainer deliberately imports a parcel. CLI validates structure, size, paths, checksums and supported schema.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 2. Local MCP process exposes an explicit import root and read-only report IDs, not arbitrary filesystem paths.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 3. Agent reads the report as **untrusted evidence**, not instructions. It checks build provenance before drawing source-level conclusions.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 4. Unknown build, incomplete tree, guessed repro step or unavailable evidence is reported as uncertainty.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 5. Code changes, commands, issue creation and model-provider uploads follow the existing project's permissions; the reporter grants none of those permissions. **Read-only MCP is not an egress guarantee:** the selected client may send returned text/images to its cloud model. Explain this before importing evidence, require the operator's informed choice, and recommend a genuinely local client/model for evidence that must not leave the machine.

heading: 6. User and developer journeys
text: 6. A synthetic regression test and the project's ordinary build/review process validate any proposed fix.

heading: 8. Evidence parcel specification
text: **Events:** nonnegative monotonic milliseconds relative to one explicitly enabled foreground collection segment, with a random ephemeral collection ID. Record trigger offset and snapshot cutoff in `capture`, so pre-trigger five-minute history is not incorrectly anchored to a report session that starts at activation. heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: ## 10. Privacy, security and consent

heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: ### 10.1 Default capture policy

heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: 1. Reporting and each optional collector activate only through explicit host configuration.

heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: 2. Screenshot and semantic-text collection are off until the host supplies a privacy/capture policy. Static screen/action IDs and nonunique build/device metadata can be enabled separately.

heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: 3. Logs, labels and attributes are sanitized **before** entering a ring buffer. Redaction runs again before persistence/export.

heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: 4. HTTP bodies, query strings, cookies, authorization headers, request IDs containing personal data and arbitrary URL path segments are not collected. Network capture uses status, method, timing and host-supplied safe route templates; raw URLs are excluded.

heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: 5. Editable/password text is never included. Sensitive descriptors/subtrees and their actions are omitted or represented by non-content omission markers.

heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: 6. Screenshot policy identifies eligible windows/regions and public/sensitive/excluded content. Unclassified or unsupported capture surfaces are omitted. A successful bitmap copy is not proof that the image is safe.

heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: 7. Sensitive regions use **opaque destructive masking**, not blur or translucent paint. Mask padding, transforms, scroll, frame/policy consistency and dynamic layout races must be tested. Mandatory host-policy masks form an irreversible sanitized editor base and cannot be undone; undo may affect only user-added annotations/masks without restoring prohibited pixels. Raw frames exist only briefly in memory, never in preview/saved state; Java/Kotlin cannot promise instantaneous secure erasure, so minimize their lifetime and copies.

heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: 8. If policy evaluation, region mapping or final redaction fails, omit the affected evidence. Privacy failure may reduce diagnostics; it must never increase collection.

heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: 9. Review shows the exact final image/text, export method and destination where known. For generic sharing, explain that the system chooser selects the recipient next; artifact approval is not recipient-specific confirmation. A content change invalidates the previous approval.

heading: 10. Privacy, security and consent
text: A host's public-label policy is an explicit trust boundary, not an automatic guarantee. Documentation must warn that screenshots and free text can still contain sensitive data, require application-specific testing and prohibit absolute “all PII is detected” claims.

text: ## 11. Reliability and exception policy

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: ### 11.1 Interpreting “try/catch everywhere” correctly

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: **Use try/catch everywhere a recoverable exception can enter an SDK-owned execution path or escape into the host:** initialization, platform/lifecycle callbacks, sensors, capture, URI handling, file/index operations, encryption, serialization, provider callbacks, network adapters, workers, desktop import and tool handlers.

evidence: No empty catch/Throwable catch; cancellation rethrown
heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: Do not sprinkle empty catch blocks around pure operations, swallow coroutine cancellation, catch all fatal errors or wrap composable invocations in invalid try/catch constructs. Defensive boundaries plus constrained inputs, ownership, isolation and tests are the standard. A catch block cannot prevent ANRs, OS process kills, native aborts or all out-of-memory failures.

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: ### 11.2 Mandatory behavior

evidence: Typed boundaries and provider isolation tests
heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: - Every **SDK-owned** exception-producing boundary converts its recoverable failures to a typed result, diagnostic code and safe user-facing state; no empty catches and no success after a failed operation. Host operations retain their own contracts: in particular, an OkHttp `chain.proceed` response/exception is propagated unchanged, never converted to an SDK result or silently replaced. Only surrounding SDK collection work is isolated; host-provider callbacks explicitly opting into evidence collection use the documented typed provider contract.

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: - Rethrow `CancellationException` immediately; preserve structured coroutine cancellation. A generic `runCatching` is prohibited in suspend/cancellable paths unless cancellation handling is explicitly correct.

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: - Catch specific expected exceptions where practical. Use a final `Exception` boundary only at identified SDK/host callback seams; catch only types the subsystem can safely handle.

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: - Do not broadly catch `Throwable`, `Error`, `VirtualMachineError`, `OutOfMemoryError` or native signals to claim recovery. Specific optional linkage failures need an isolated, documented strategy; v1 avoids JNI dependencies.

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: - Cancellation and cleanup use `finally` and scoped ownership; cleanup failures must not replace the original outcome or leak a resource.

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: - Each optional collector can fail independently. If screenshot capture fails, retain description; if semantic collection fails, retain approved non-semantic evidence. If privacy fails, omit evidence; if serialization fails, do not export a misleading partial archive.

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: - Reporter callbacks must not throw into host callbacks. The OkHttp adapter must preserve the host's response/failure and avoid consuming streams.

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: - Use supervised SDK-owned jobs so one collector cannot cancel the host scope. Supervision does not handle exceptions by itself; child jobs still need result handling and a sanitized last-resort diagnostic hook.

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
text: - No blocking disk/network operations on the UI thread; try/catch does not make blocking safe.

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
notes: Reporter strings moved to resources with an additional locale
text: - Production UI uses localized error resources and recoverable action states, never raw exception messages. Diagnostic records use safe codes/class names; causes may contain secrets and cannot be logged verbatim.

heading: 11. Reliability and exception policy
notes: Compose state/failure paths represented; tests cover form/review/recreation
text: - Compose UI represents failures as state. Do not use try/catch around composable calls as an error-boundary mechanism. Validate arguments, isolate effects, keep rendering simple and test release behavior.

heading: 17. Licensing and community governance

A host application's own `AGPL-3.0-or-later` status does not automatically determine this new project's license. text: First-party SDK, tooling, server code, schemas and documentation use the declared project license; preserve third-party licenses/notices. heading: 17. Licensing and community governance
text: ### 17.2 SDK adoption implications

heading: 17. Licensing and community governance
text: AGPL is strong copyleft. An Android app that links/includes this SDK may form a combined/derivative work and generally cannot assume it can remain proprietary merely because the SDK is an AAR. Distribution can require corresponding source, notices and compatible licensing for the covered combined work. **No proprietary-linking exception is granted.** Explain this prominently before installation; get qualified legal review for disputed integration/distribution cases.

heading: 17. Licensing and community governance
text: AGPL Section 13 additionally requires a modified version supporting remote interaction to prominently offer corresponding source to users interacting with it over a network. It is not a rule that every program making any HTTP request must disclose all unrelated software, nor is it a ban on charging money. Preserve distribution/source rights and applicable notice obligations. A future hosted component must implement an appropriate source offer for the deployed covered version.

heading: 17. Licensing and community governance
notes: No copyright claim over user reports.
text: The data format is not a mechanism for granting the project copyright over a user's bug report. Users retain applicable rights in their submitted data. Independently implemented consumers and interpretation of code-linking boundaries require proper legal assessment; do not promise an AGPL exemption merely because a component is in another process.
